title: The Crash Inside a Winning Year

beats.text: In one day, the market lost almost a quarter of its value. The year still ended up.
October nineteenth, nineteen eighty-seven. You're Ned, savings all in stocks.
The opening bell rings, and the Dow drops.
By the close: down twenty-two point six percent.
Ned stares until his coffee grows a skin.
How does a market lose a quarter of itself before dinner?
You see, it's a packed theater. Everyone's plan: if someone stands, run.
Big funds used a new portfolio insurance: computers that sell when prices fall.
Selling pushed prices down. Lower prices triggered more selling.
So Ned sells everything at the bottom.
But by New Year's Eve, the Dow was higher than in January.
Ned lost money in a year the market went up.

facts.claim: Black Monday was October 19, 1987; the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 508 points, or 22.6 percent, in one session (almost a quarter)
The Dow crashed at the opening bell
Portfolio insurance, a new product popular with institutional investors, used futures/options and computerized programs that sold as prices fell, so losses led to further rounds of selling
Despite Black Monday the Dow ended 1987 higher than it began (about 1,897 on Jan 2 to 1,939 on Dec 31; +2.26% for the year)
Theater-fire analogy for the crash was used at the time (Andrew Grove quote in the Fed essay); Ned is a fictional everyman

caption:
October 19, 1987: the Dow falls 22.6% in a single day.
Computers sold because prices fell, and prices fell because computers sold.
Then the year ended higher than it began.
